text: The tradecraft is domestic: a house to learn, a telephone in the hallway, a husband who must never notice the pause before an answer. Meghna Gulzar sets her thriller inside a Pakistani officer's household during the 1971 war and hands the work to a young woman whose whole assignment is to be unremarkable at breakfast. The suspense runs on chores. Two hours and eighteen minutes are long enough for a marriage to become real, which is the trap laid here: affection accumulates across a line neither person drew, and every kindness has to be filed and put to use. For long stretches nothing detonates. The strain shows across a dinner table instead, in a sentence that arrives half a second late, in the arithmetic of a woman counting what she has already sent home.

A police inspector has driven his own superior into an asylum, and the film treats this as an engineering problem rather than a punchline. Dreyfus gets out, and the apparatus he builds to remove Clouseau is scaled so far past its target that the joke keeps annexing more of the planet. What holds it together is audible timing: a door, a beat, a crash, and then the silence after the crash, which is where Blake Edwards actually works. The gags are choreographed to the frame rather than to a list, so the room, the furniture, and one man's blindness to both do the labor. A hundred and three minutes of falling over, built with the internal logic of a heist, and the Writers Guild cited the screenplay, which for this kind of picture is an odd compliment.

The barrier is a language, and the family already has the money. Mita and Raj Batra are wealthy by the standards of Chandni Chowk and inadmissible by the standards of the Delhi schools they want their daughter inside, where the entrance interview is really an audit of the parents. Saket Chaudhary plays it as comedy, because at close range class humiliation is mostly farce: coaching sessions for adults, borrowed vocabulary, a wife certain the problem can be bought off. Two hours and twelve minutes is generous for a story about admission forms, and the time goes into machinery: which gate, which address, what a shopkeeping family is permitted to sound like in a room built to hear it. Filmfare's best-film vote went to a picture whose snobs are selling exactly what its heroes are trying to buy.

Sixty-six minutes is barely a feature, and it is the entire container for a boy's grief. Claude Barras animates what comes after a mother's death: a police officer named Raymond who keeps turning up, a foster home in which every other child arrived by a route just as bad. Choosing animation is not a softening. It lets faces stay simple enough for a child to read while the situations underneath them stay adult, and it keeps the film from either flinching or leering. The Cristal at Annecy went to a story that spends its middle stretch on bunk assignments, a new arrival, and who sits where at breakfast, the ordinary sociability of an institution, which is how a group of damaged children becomes a working society. None of that is hurried, in a film with no time to spare.

The young man at the center is developmentally disabled, and the science fiction exists to get him a friend. Rakesh Roshan's visitor is not a threat to be repelled or a specimen to be studied; it is company for someone the town has decided to talk around, and that single reassignment bends every convention the genre arrives with. A hundred and sixty-five minutes leaves room for three pictures in sequence: small-town comedy, wonder story, then something nearer to adventure. The seams are managed by mood rather than plot mechanics. Underneath sit two much older anxieties, a mother's question about who will look after her son and a neighborhood's habit of cruelty toward anyone slow, and the spectacle when it comes is put entirely at the service of the first.

A woman with money enlists in the United States Army on a whim, and the film's real problem is what to do once the whim wears off. Howard Zieff needs her to be genuinely unequipped - for the barracks, the mud, the shouting, the absence of anyone paid to be pleasant to her - before he can get interested in what she becomes. The Academy noticed the acting and the writing, which is the right split: a script assembled out of humiliations, a performance assembled out of posture, slowly corrected. Basic training is only the first movement. What follows is harder to keep funny, since it involves a woman discovering she can survive being ordinary and then deciding whether ordinary is what she wants. The comedy of manners never leaves. It only changes which manners look absurd.

Four identical plaid overnight bags, and nobody is holding the right one. Peter Bogdanovich builds ninety-four minutes out of that single mistake and refuses to add a second idea, which is the discipline of the thing: the audience always knows where each bag is, the characters never do, and the distance between those two conditions is the whole supply of laughter. Farce is an architecture problem. Doors have to sit where the wrong people will keep almost meeting, and the timing has to be exact to the frame or the machine reads as noise. Not every bag is full of laundry, and that is how the crime gets in, and why the chasing stays serious to everyone inside it and weightless to everyone watching. The romance runs on the same mechanism, two people colliding on a schedule.

The story arrives secondhand, told by comedians over lunch at the Carnegie Deli, shaped by retelling before a frame of it is dramatized. That frame does more than it appears to. Everything here is already an anecdote, and Danny Rose is a man in the process of becoming one. He represents acts that cannot work, a one-legged tap dancer among them, and his one client with a career on the mend, the singer Lou Canova, pulls him into a matter with the mob that was never his to be in. Eighty-four minutes, no fat. The comedy runs on loyalty played completely straight: Danny keeps making the choice a better-connected man would decline, and Woody Allen declines to call him a fool for it. Underneath is the economics of small-time show business, where a commission and a favor are the same transaction.

One slap, in front of guests, and then two hours and twenty-four minutes of people explaining why it is not worth leaving over. Anubhav Sinha builds the film out of that disproportion: the act takes a second, the argument about the act consumes a marriage, two households, and the patience of everyone who assumed the thing would be settled by morning. The pressure that follows is not physical. It is domestic and financial and unrelenting - a house that has to keep running, advice arriving from people who love her, all of it pointed in the direction of staying. Filmfare's acting award went to a performance built almost entirely out of withholding. Sinha keeps his camera at the height of ordinary rooms, where the sentence about it having happened only once does most of the damage.

A rehearsal room is a poor place to keep a secret, since everyone in it is paid to watch other people's bodies. Yash Chopra sets his triangle inside a working dance troupe, where the man both women are arranged around is also the director they answer to, and where feeling has a professional pretext for being expressed in public. Three hours. That length is not padding; it is the license to let a friendship curdle slowly enough that the exact week it changes can be felt. Nisha has loved Rahul long enough for it to have hardened into a habit, which is worse than a wound. Pooja is engaged to somebody else. The subject, finally, is the etiquette of unspoken things - the seating, the timing, who gets told first - and how choreography lets people say what they have agreed not to say.

Filed as family entertainment, and every failure in it belongs to an adult. Michael Ritchie hands the worst team in an ultra-competitive California little league to a coach who is past it and short of money, and the comedy comes out of the gap between what the grown-ups need from a season and what a child can supply. The children are shrewd judges of who is lying to them. That is the engine: authority has to be earned, by a man with nothing else left to trade, in front of the one audience a career cannot impress. Nobody improves on schedule. A hundred and two minutes go mostly to the organization of the thing, rosters and standings and parents at the fence, and to how much of a child's afternoon belongs to somebody else's ambition.

The prize is a bicycle race between colleges, and the film takes the better part of three hours to reach the start line. Mansoor Khan uses the delay properly. Sanjay is careless in the way only a young man with an older brother to absorb the consequences can afford to be, and the injury that puts him on the bike arrives less as an opportunity than as a bill. The rivalry runs between schools that stand for different amounts of money, which gives every practice session a second meaning without anyone having to name it. This is a drama with a sports engine, so the race works as a deadline rather than a subject. What lasts is the sibling material, the particular irritation of being loved by a brother more disciplined than himself.
